entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Nicholas of Ilok (died 1477) was a preeminent Hungarian nobleman and military commander whose career spanned the mid-15th century, a period marked by intense conflict with the encroaching Ottoman Empire. As a loyal vassal and trusted lieutenant of King Matthias Corvinus, he wielded immense power across a vast swathe of the Hungarian Kingdom's southern and eastern frontiers, holding the crucial titles of Ban of Croatia, Slavonia, and Dalmatia, Ban of Macsó, and Voivode of Transylvania. His strategic importance lay in his role as a bulwark against Ottoman expansion, defending vital territories and attempting to stabilize the volatile Balkan borderlands.

Nicholas's tenure as a magnate saw him engage in numerous military campaigns against the Ottomans, most notably participating in the recapture of Jajce in Bosnia in 1463, a strategic fortress crucial for Hungarian defense. In recognition of his loyalty and military prowess, King Matthias Corvinus appointed him titular King of Bosnia in 1471, a move intended to reassert Hungarian suzerainty over the region and create a stable buffer state following the Ottoman conquest of the Bosnian Kingdom in 1463. Although his claim to the Bosnian throne was largely symbolic due to ongoing Ottoman occupation, he actively governed the remaining Hungarian-held territories of Bosnia, reinforcing fortifications and organizing defenses against further incursions.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Nicholas of Ilok was a pivotal figure in the defense of the Hungarian Kingdom against the Ottoman Empire, delaying their advance into Central Europe and stabilizing critical border regions for several decades. His efforts as Ban and titular King of Bosnia directly impacted the geopolitical landscape of the Balkans in the late 15th century.
